# Volume 5 — CHAPTER IV. THE MANSE CHILDREN

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Aunt Martha could be—and indeed was—an exceedingly bad housekeeper, just as the Rev. John Knox Ashdown could be—and indeed was—an exceptionally absent-minded, lenient man. Nevertheless, nobody could deny that the manse of Glen St. Agnes possessed an exceedingly cozy and endearing quality, notwithstanding its clutter. It was felt even by the discerning housewives of the Glen, whose opinions were unwittingly softened as a result. This appeal might have stemmed partly from fortuitous details—the lush vines wrapping around its gray, weatherboarded walls, the welcoming acacias and balm-of-gileads surrounding it with the familiarity of long-time friends, and the lovely vistas of sand-dunes and harbour visible from its forward windows. Yet those features had also existed during the era of Mr. Ashdown’s predecessor, a time when the manse was the most proper, orderly, and gloomy dwelling in the Glen. Consequently, a great deal of the merit belonged to the character of its current occupants. An aura of mirth and fellowship enveloped the place; its doors remained constantly unlatched; and the internal and external realms met. In the Glen St. Agnes manse, love served as the sole rule.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0000 }

According to the members of his flock, Mr. Ashdown indulged his offspring too much. It was quite probable that he was guilty of this. What remains beyond doubt is that he lacked the heart to reprimand them. “They have no mother,” he was accustomed to remark softly to himself, uttering a sigh whenever an exceptionally blatant misdeed was brought inescapably to his attention. Yet he remained ignorant of most of their misconduct. He was a member of the class of visionaries. Although his study's windows faced the cemetery, while he walked back and forth across the floor, pondering profoundly upon the eternal nature of the spirit, he failed entirely to notice Tobias and Rupert joyously playing leap-frog across the horizontal monuments in that resting place of deceased Methodists. Mr. Ashdown experienced sporadic, sharp epiphanies that his sons and daughters lacked the physical and moral care they had received prior to his wife's passing, and he maintained an ever-present, faint awareness that the residence and food diverged greatly under Aunt Martha’s care compared to their quality during Cecilia’s lifetime. Otherwise, his existence transpired amid volumes of literature and theoretical concepts; consequently, even though his garments were rarely swept clean of dust, and even though the women of the Glen deduced, owing to the alabaster-like paleness of his chiseled face and delicate hands, that he was perpetually undernourished, he did not lead a miserable life.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0001 }

Should a cemetery ever deserve to be deemed a happy location, the ancient Methodist cemetery located in Glen St. Agnes could perhaps be designated as such. On the opposite side of the Methodist church lay the modern cemetery, which was an orderly, correct, and gloomy area; nevertheless, the ancient one had been abandoned for such a duration to the benevolent and merciful care of Nature that it was rendered exceedingly agreeable.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0002 }

A stone and sod embankment, crowned with a gray and rickety fence, enclosed three of its sides. Beyond this wall stood a line of lofty fir trees bearing dense, fragrant branches. Constructed by the initial inhabitants of the Glen, the embankment was ancient enough to possess beauty, as mosses and verdant plants sprouted from its cracks, violets bloomed purple at its foot during the initial days of spring, and asters alongside golden-rod created a fall splendor within its nooks. Small ferns gathered closely together among its rocks, while an expansive bracken shot up in places.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0003 }

No fence or dyke existed on the eastern side. In that direction, the graveyard wandered into a young fir plantation, constantly creeping closer to the graves and darkening to the east into a dense wood. The air was perpetually filled with the sea’s harp-like voices, alongside the music of ancient gray trees, while the bird choruses in the elms encircling the two churches sang of life rather than death on spring mornings. The old graveyard was loved by the Ashdown children.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0004 }

Over the caved-in burial sites, mint, “garden-spruce,” and ivy with blue eyes proliferated wildly. Beside the fir forest, in the sandy nook, blueberry shrubs developed in great abundance. The changing styles of headstones across three generations could be observed in that place, beginning with the level, rectangular, red sandstone flags belonging to early pioneers, progressing through the era of clutching hands and weeping willows, up to the most recent horrors consisting of covered urns and towering “monuments.” A particular example of this last style, which was the largest and most hideous in the burial ground, honored the remembrance of an individual named Hector Twiss, who was born into the Methodist faith but had married a Presbyterian woman from the Fairlie family. She had forced his conversion to Presbyterianism and forced him to strictly adhere to Presbyterian ways throughout his entire life. However, upon his death, she lacked the courage to condemn him to an isolated plot in the cross-harbor Presbyterian cemetery. His relatives were all interred within the Methodist graveyard; consequently, Hector Twiss returned to his own kin in demise, and his surviving wife found comfort in putting up a stone that proved more expensive than what any Methodist could pay for. The Ashdown children despised this marker, though they did not quite understand the reason, yet they adored the ancient, level, bench-shaped slabs that had high weeds sprouting wildly around them. For one reason, those offered pleasant places to sit. Every one of them was seated upon a single slab at that moment. Tobias, having grown weary of playing leap frog, was making music with a jew’s-harp. Rupert was intently studying an unusual insect he had come across; Ida was attempting to fashion a garment for a doll, and Grace, supporting her weight backward on her thin brown wrists, was moving her unclothed feet in an energetic rhythm to the jew’s-harp.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0005 }

Tobias possessed the dark hair and expansive dark eyes of his father, though his own eyes sparkled rather than appeared visionary. Grace, who was born after him, carried her loveliness with the casual radiance of a blossom. Her eyes were golden-brown, her ringlets were golden-brown, and her cheeks were deep red. Her frequent laughter displeased her father’s flock, and she had outraged elderly Mrs. Taylor, who was the melancholic widow of multiple deceased spouses, when she pertly asserted—and right in the church-porch no less—“The world isn’t a vale of tears, Mrs. Taylor. It’s a world of laughter.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0006 }

Young, visionary Ida rarely giggled. No wild curls appeared in her plaits of limp, pitch-black hair, and a hint of longing and sadness rested within her slanted, deep-blue eyes. Her lips possessed a habit of parting above her minute ivory teeth, and now and then a bashful, thoughtful grin spread across her delicate features. Far more touchy regarding the views of others than Grace, she felt a troubling awareness that their lifestyle was somehow flawed. She desired to fix things, yet lacked the knowledge to do so. On occasion she wiped the dust from the furnishings—though she located the rag very rarely since its location changed constantly. Furthermore, whenever the garment brush could be located she attempted to clean her father’s finest clothing on Saturdays, and on one occasion attached an absent button using thick white yarn. As Mr. Ashdown attended chapel the following morning, each woman present spotted that button, disrupting the harmony of the Ladies’ Aid for a month or more.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0007 }

Rupert possessed his deceased mother’s unafraid, straightforward, luminous, dark-blue eyes, as well as her golden-glinted brown hair. The hidden ways of insects were known to him, and he held a kind of brotherhood with beetles and bees. Ida always avoided sitting close to him since she could never tell what weird beast he might have hidden on his person. Because Rupert had once brought a juvenile garter snake into bed, Tobias declined to share a bed with him; consequently, Rupert occupied his old crib, where he could not extend his legs because it was too brief, and shared his sleep with odd companions. When Aunt Martha smoothed the blankets of that bed, it was probably fortunate that her sight was failing. On the whole, they formed a merry, endearing small group, and Cecilia Ashdown’s heart surely suffered a terrible pang as she confronted the certainty of her departure from them.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0008 }

“If you happened to be a Methodist, in what place would you prefer your burial to be?” Grace inquired brightly.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0009 }

An intriguing area of conjecture was revealed by this.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0010 }

“Options are limited because the location is crowded,” Tobias remarked. “I suppose I would prefer the corner beside the street. That way, I would be able to listen to the passing teams and the conversations of the people.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0011 }

“That small depression beneath the weeping birch would suit me,” Ida remarked. “Birds gather so frequently in that birch, and their morning songs are wonderfully exuberant.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0012 }

“I would choose the Porter plot containing the large number of buried children, since I enjoy plenty of companionship,” Grace remarked. “Where would you go, Rupert?”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0013 }

“I would prefer to forgo burial entirely,” Rupert remarked, “yet were it required, the ant-bed would be my choice, since ants prove terribly fascinating.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0014 }

“How extraordinarily good everyone interred in this place must have been,” remarked Ida, having spent time studying the eulogistic old tombstone inscriptions. “Not one wicked person appears to lie within this entire cemetery. It seems Methodists are superior to Presbyterians, when all is said and done.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0015 }

“Perhaps bad people are buried by the Methodists in the same manner as cats,” Rupert suggested. “It could be that they do not take the trouble of bringing them to the graveyard whatsoever.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0016 }

“Nonsense,” Grace remarked. “Ida, the individuals interred in this place were no superior to anyone else. However, once a person has died, you are required to speak only favorably about him, otherwise his ghost will return to haunt you. That was imparted to me by Aunt Martha. When I queried father regarding its accuracy, his gaze simply passed right through me as he murmured, ‘True? True? What is truth? What is truth, O jesting Pilate?’ Based on his response, I decided it was bound to be true.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0017 }

“I wonder whether Mr. Hector Twiss would return to haunt me if I tossed a rock at the urn resting upon his gravestone,” Tobias said.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0018 }

“Mrs. Twiss would,” Grace giggled. “She simply observes us in church the way a cat observes mice. This past Sunday I pulled a face at her nephew, who pulled one back at me, and her glare was quite something to behold. I bet she cuffed his ears once they left. Mrs. Ambrose Kerr informed me that we must not displease her under any circumstances, otherwise I would have pulled a face at her as well!”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0019 }

“People claim that Kit Carrow made a face at her a single time and she refused to see his father from then on, even during the period her husband was on his deathbed,” Tobias remarked. “I am curious about the nature of the Carrow gang.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0020 }

“Their appearance appealed to me,” Grace remarked. When the Carrow young ones had come that afternoon, the manse kids had been present at the station. “Kit’s appearance was particularly pleasing to me.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0021 }

“Tobias mentioned, “It’s said at school that Edmund is a sissy.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0022 }

“I doubt that,” stated Ida, who had considered Edmund quite good-looking.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0023 }

“At any rate, he composes poetry. Bertie Shakespeare Drew informed me that he earned the award provided by the teacher the previous year for composing a verse. Bertie’s mother believed he ought to have received the award owing to his name, yet Bertie stated he was unable to compose poetry for the life of him, regardless of his name.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0024 }

“It seems likely that we’ll become familiar with them the moment they start attending school,” Grace pondered. “My wish is that the girls prove pleasant. The majority of the girls in this area do not appeal to me. Slow and dull describes even the pleasant ones. However, the Carrow twins appear cheerful. My impression was that twins invariably resembled each other, yet these two do not. The one with red hair strikes me as the pleasantest.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0025 }

“I approved of the way their mother looked,” Ida remarked, uttering a brief sigh. Ida felt jealous of every child who had a mother. Her own mother had passed away when she was merely six, yet within her spirit she guarded invaluable recollections—similar to precious gems—of morning play and dusk hugs, of a gentle tone, affectionate eyes, and a laugh that was unmatched in its sweetness and merriment.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0026 }

“People claim that she is different from everyone else,” Tobias remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0027 }

“Grace mentioned that, according to Mrs. Elliot, the reason was her failure to ever truly reach adulthood.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0028 }

“Mrs. Kerr is not as tall as she is.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0029 }

“Indeed, indeed, yet she is like that on the interior—according to Mrs. Elliot, Mrs. Carrow simply remained a young girl on the inside.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0030 }

“What is that scent?” Rupert cut in, taking a breath through his nose.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0031 }

Every one of them caught the scent at this point. Rising through the unmoving night air, a delightfully appealing fragrance drifted upward from the small, wooded hollow beneath the hill where the manse stood.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0032 }

“Hearing that gives me an appetite,” Tobias remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0033 }

“For our evening meal, we had nothing but bread and molasses, and for our mid-day meal, we had the exact same thing cold,” Ida said mournfully.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0034 }

It was Aunt Martha’s custom to boil a big piece of mutton at the beginning of the week and present it daily, unheated and fatty, for as long as any remained. Grace, during a flash of creativity, had assigned to this the title of “ditto”, and it was constantly called by that name in the manse.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0035 }

“Let us head over to find the source of that odor,” Tobias suggested.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0036 }

Every one of them leaped to their feet, romped across the grass with the uninhibited energy of newborn pups, scrambled over a barrier, and rushed down the moss-covered incline, led by the appetizing aroma that continuously intensified. After a short period, they reached the innermost sanctuary of Fern Hollow out of breath, at the precise moment when the Carrow children were on the verge of offering grace and consuming their meal.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0037 }

They stopped in a hesitant manner. Ida regretted their sudden haste, yet Izzy Carrow could handle that situation just as easily as any other. Displaying a friendly smile, she advanced toward them.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0038 }

“I believe I recognize you,” she uttered. “You are from the manse, aren’t you?”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0039 }

Dimples creasing her face, Grace gave a nod.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0040 }

“Having caught the scent of your trout being prepared, we were curious about it.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0041 }

“Sit yourself down so you can assist us in eating them,” Izzy said.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0042 }

“Perhaps you do not possess extra for your own needs,” Tobias remarked, gazing with craving upon the metal dish.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0043 }

“We have plenty—three for each of us,” Kit stated. “Take a seat.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0044 }

Without further formality, the entire group took their seats upon moss-covered rocks. Long and joyful was that banquet. If Bess and Izzy had been aware of what Grace and Ida were fully conscious of—namely, that a pair of little mice resided within Rupert’s coat pocket—they would likely have perished from fright. However, because they remained unaware, no harm befell them. What better place exists for people to become truly familiar with one another than around a dining table? By the time the final trout was eaten, the kids from the manse and the kids from Hollowmere had become devoted companions and confederates. It felt as though their acquaintance had lasted forever and would endure indefinitely. The lineage of Joseph acknowledged its own kind.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0045 }

The pasts of their brief lives were recounted by them. Brierley and Grey Shutters, Fern Hollow lore, and the small home beside the harbour coast where Kit came into the world were made known to the manse children. Juneford, the former home of the Ashdowns prior to their arrival at the Glen, along with Ida’s cherished doll possessing a single eye and Grace’s tamed rooster, were told to the Hollowmere children.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0046 }

It irked Grace that others mocked her habit of stroking a rooster. Her fondness for the Carrows stemmed from their unhesitating acceptance of it.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0047 }

“In my opinion, a fine-looking rooster such as Adam makes a pet that is every bit as pleasant as a cat or dog,” she remarked. “No one would think it strange if he were a canary. Furthermore, I raised him starting when he was a tiny, small, yellow chick. He was given to me by Mrs. Johnson at Juneford. His brothers and sisters had all been slain by a weasel. I named him for her spouse. Dolls and cats never appealed to me. Cats have too much slyness, while dolls lack life.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0048 }

“Who resides in that home far up in that direction?” Tobias inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0049 }

“The Miss Ainslies—Clementine and Harriet,” Bess replied. “Music lessons from Miss Clementine will be taken by Izzy and me this summer.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0050 }

With an affection too mild to be jealousy, Ida looked upon the fortunate twins. Ah, if only music lessons were possible for her! That desire remained a secret dream of her quiet young existence. Nevertheless, the idea was never entertained by anyone.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0051 }

“Miss Clementine is exceptionally sweet and her clothes are always so pretty,” Izzy remarked. “The shade of her hair matches fresh molasses taffy,” she added longingly—because Izzy, following the example of her mother, had never accepted her own reddish locks.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0052 }

“Miss Harriet is also someone I like,” Bess said. “When she attended church, she would constantly hand out candies to me. Izzy, however, fears her.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0053 }

“She possesses such dark brows alongside that immensely deep voice of hers,” Izzy remarked. “Oh, Julian Treleaven was so terrified of her during his early years! According to Mother, Miss Harriet chanced to be present, seated directly in back of them, on the very first Sunday that Mrs. Treleaven took him to church. And as soon as Julian set eyes on her, he simply shrieked repeatedly to the point where Mrs. Treleaven was forced to lift him up and take him outside.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0054 }

“Who is Mrs. Treleaven?” Ida inquired with wonder.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0055 }

“Oh, the Treleavens aren't residents here. They merely arrive during the summer months. Furthermore, they will not be visiting this summer. Their residence is in that small cottage far, far down along the harbour coast, which used to be my father and mother's home. I would love for you to behold Damaris Treleaven. She resembles a painting.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0056 }

“Mrs. Treleaven is someone I have heard of,” Grace interrupted. “It was Bertie Shakespeare Drew who mentioned her to me. A deceased man was her husband for fourteen years, after which he returned to life.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0057 }

“Nonsense,” Bess remarked. “It does not happen like that in the slightest. Bertie Shakespeare is incapable of getting a single detail right. The entire account is known to me and I will share it with you eventually, though not at present, as it is excessively lengthy and we must head back home. Mother disapproves of our being outdoors at a late hour on damp evenings such as these.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0058 }

No one gave any thought to whether the minister's children remained in the moisture or had come indoors. Aunt Martha had retired to her bed by that time, and the minister remained far too engrossed in his thoughts regarding the soul's immortality to recall that the physical frame was mortal. Nonetheless, they also returned to their dwelling, carrying thoughts of approaching happy moments within their minds.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0059 }

“Fern Hollow strikes me as being even more pleasant than the cemetery,” Ida remarked. “And those precious Carrows are simply wonderful to me. Being able to care for folks is so delightful, given how frequently it’s impossible. It was stated by Father in his sermon this past Sunday that our love should extend to all people. Yet how is that achievable? In what way could anyone feel love for Mrs. Hector Twiss?”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0060 }

“Oh, father merely uttered that from the pulpit,” Grace said lightly. “He possesses too much judgment to actually believe it elsewhere.”
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0061 }

Except for Kit, who stole off briefly on an isolated journey to a distant section of Fern Hollow, the Carrow youngsters walked up to Hollowmere. Mayflowers bloomed in that location, and Kit always remembered to bring his mother a bunch of them for as long as they remained.
{: #nw-v05-c04-p0062 }
